question: A 50-year-old man presents with acute monoarthritis of the right first metatarsophalangeal joint with severe pain and erythema. Which SINGLE investigation is MOST specific for confirming the diagnosis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CRP confirms inflammation but is non-specific; it will be elevated in gout, septic arthritis, and other inflammatory conditions without distinguishing among them.

Serum uric acid may be normal during an acute gout attack (levels fall acutely due to uricosuric effect of inflammation) and elevated in asymptomatic hyperuricaemia — it is not specific for confirming acute gout.

answers.text: Synovial fluid microscopy for negatively birefringent crystals under polarised light

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Gout crystals (monosodium urate) are needle-shaped and NEGATIVELY birefringent under polarised light microscopy. This is the definitive investigation, distinguishing gout from pseudogout (positively birefringent calcium pyrophosphate crystals) and septic arthritis.
ANA is a screening test for systemic autoimmune diseases (SLE, Sjögren's); it has no role in the workup of acute monoarthritis of the first MTP joint, which is classic podagra (gout).

overallFeedback.feedback: For acute monoarthritis, especially of the first MTP joint, the definitive investigation is synovial fluid polarised light microscopy. Remember the crystal birefringence rule: gout = NEGATIVELY birefringent (yellow when parallel to the slow axis); pseudogout = POSITIVELY birefringent (blue when parallel).
Excellent. The gold standard for diagnosing gout is synovial fluid analysis showing needle-shaped, negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals under polarised light microscopy.
